newsitem.title: THAILAND: Merger collapse means rocky week ahead in Thailand.
newsitem.headline: Merger collapse means rocky week ahead in Thailand.

text.p: The collapse of a planned mega-merger between cash-strapped Thai finance firm Finance One Plc and Thai Danu Bank ensures a rocky week ahead for the country's financial markets, analysts said.

Fallout from the collapse could include a run on deposits by Finance One customers, a major sell-off on the battered stock market and a sea change in central bank guidelines on consolidation in the ailing Thai finance sector, they said.
The Bank of Thailand has ordered a probe into Finance One to determine if its management had committed fraud, The Nation newspaper quoted the central bank governor as saying.
"If we discover any fraud, we'll take drastic action to protect the interests of innoncent depositors and creditors," governor Rerngchai Marakanond told the newspaper.

Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan put a brave face on the situation, saying on Sunday the central bank was prepared to help out Finance One with funding if it could not raise capital through a rights issue.
Finance One was ordered to raise capital by 8.28 billion baht ($318 million) last Friday through a two-for-one rights issue at 7.50 baht a share.
"The central bank via its rehabilitation fund is ready to buy Finance One's new shares if existing shareholders don't want to take those shares," Amnuay said.
The stock exchange was to decide early on Monday whether to allow trading to resume in suspended Finance One shares, while Thai Danu asked for a trading resumption on Wednesday.

The central bank was due to hold a news conference on Monday to announce new monetary measures and guidelines for consolidation in the finance sector, which has been hit by an economic downturn, tight liquidity and heavy loans exposure to the depressed property sector.
Two months of merger talks collapsed last Friday when Finance One and Thai Danu said they could not link up because of complex tax and legal issues.
The failure embarrassed the finance ministry and the central bank, which had blessed the deal.
The merger, if it had taken place, would have been Thailand's biggest between financial institutions.
The failure could shake public confidence in the stability of Thailand's 91 finance companies, some of which face severe liquidity problems, analysts said.
Although the failure of the merger was largely expected by the markets, it was seen as another blow to the weak finance sector which the authorities have been revamping recently.
"The merger collapse should be largely discounted by the market but there may be some who were not that prepared for it," said Graham Catterwell, country manager for Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"It's another major body blow to the weak finance sector at a time when it does not need it."
Other analysts said the worst was yet to come for the finance sector.
If property prices fell sharply in coming months as a result of a four-year depression and glut, a major finance sector meltdown could result, they said.
The willingness of the central bank to assist Finance One could calm investor sentiment somewhat on the firm's deposits and shares, they added.
"Everyone knows the Bank of Thailand will step in and help them. They also pretty much knew the merger had broken down," said an analyst at a foreign brokerage.

The unsuccessful merger may have spelt the end of any future such deals between financial institutions because Thai tax law and other legal issues related to mergers appeared more complicated than previously thought, analysts said.
